etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English arm, from Old English earm, from Proto-West Germanic *arm, from Proto-Germanic *armaz (“arm”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“a fitting, joint; arm, forequarter”), a suffixed form of *h₂er- (“to join, fit together”).

definitions.definition: (anatomy) The portion of the upper human appendage, from the shoulder to the wrist and sometimes including the hand.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 19, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: When Timothy and Julia hurried up the staircase to the bedroom floor, where a considerable commotion was taking place, Tim took Barry Leach with him. He had him gripped firmly by the arm, since he felt it was not safe to let him loose, and he had no immediate idea what to do with him.

quote.citation: 1991, “Jesus Christ Pose”, in Chris Cornell (lyrics), Soundgarden (music), Badmotorfinger, performed by Soundgarden, Track 4:
quote.text: And you stare at meIn your Jesus Christ poseArms held outLike you've been carrying a load

definitions.definition: (anatomy) The extended portion of the upper limb, from the shoulder to the elbow.
A limb, or locomotive or prehensile organ, of an invertebrate animal.
The part of a piece of clothing that covers the arm.

quote.citation: 1851 November 14, Herman Melville, “Chapter 100”, in Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, 1st American edition, New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers; London: Richard Bentley, →OCLC, page 485:
quote.text: […]  one arm of this jacket streamed behind him like the broidered arm of a huzzar’s surcoat.

quote.citation: 1970, J. G. Farrell, Troubles‎[1], New York: Knopf, published 1971, page 340:
quote.text: […]  he noticed that a dark stain had appeared under the arm of her grey silk dress.

quote.citation: 2000, Zadie Smith, White Teeth, London: Hamish Hamilton, →ISBN, page 82:
quote.text: Samad made a grab for the boy and caught him by the arm of his shirt.

definitions.definition: A long, narrow, more or less rigid part of an object extending from the main part or centre of the object, such as the armrest of an armchair, a crane, a pair of spectacles or a pair of compasses.
(geography) A bay or inlet off a main body of water.
A branch of an organization.

quote.citation: 2018 April 25, Ron Nixon, “Scandals and Investigations, but Few Arrests, for Air Marshals Program”, in The New York Times‎[2]:
quote.text: Congress has asked the Government Accountability Office, its investigative arm, to review the workplace complaints raised by air marshals, said Charles Young, a spokesman for the office.

definitions.definition: (figurative) Power; might; strength; support.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Isaiah 52:1:
quote.text: To whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?

definitions.definition: (baseball, slang) A pitcher
(genetics) One of the two parts of a chromosome.
A group of patients in a medical trial.
(obsolete) To take by the arm; to take up in one's arms.

quote.citation: 1611 April (first recorded performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Cymbeline”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii]:
quote.text: And make him with our pikes and partisans / A grave: come, arm him.

quote.citation: 1613–1614 (date written), John Fletcher, William Shak[e]speare, The Two Noble Kinsmen: […], London:  […]  Tho[mas] Cotes, for Iohn Waterson;  […], published 1634, →OCLC, (please specify the page), (please specify the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: Arm your prize; / I know you will not lose him.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English arm (“poor, wretched”), from Old English earm (“poor, miserable, pitiful, wretched”), from Proto-West Germanic *arm, from Proto-Germanic *armaz (“poor”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁erm- (“poor, ill”).

definitions.definition: (UK dialectal, chiefly Scotland) Poor; lacking in riches or wealth.
(UK dialectal, chiefly Scotland) To be pitied; pitiful; wretched.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Back-formation from arms (plural), from Middle English armes, from Old French armes, from Latin arma (“weapons”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er-mo-, a suffixed form of *h₂er- (“to fit together”), hence ultimately cognate with etymology 1.

definitions.definition: (usually used in the plural) A weapon.

quote.citation: 1789, Second Amendment to the United States Constitution:
quote.text: A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.

quote.citation: 1881–1882, Robert Louis Stevenson, Treasure Island, London; Paris: Cassell & Company, published 14 November 1883, →OCLC:
quote.text: The next thing I laid hold of was a brace of pistols, and as I already had a powder horn and bullets, I felt myself well supplied with arms.

definitions.definition: (in the plural) Heraldic bearings or insignia.
(in the plural, obsolete) War; hostilities; deeds or exploits of war. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
(transitive) To supply with armour or (later especially) weapons.

quote.citation: 2015, George R. R. Martin, A Dance with Dragons, Bantam, →ISBN, page 593:
quote.text: They were arming them with spears and shields, putting iron halfhelms on their heads, and arraying them along the inner wall, a rank of snowy sentinels. "Lord Winter has joined us with his levies," one of the sentries [said].

definitions.definition: (transitive, figurative) To supply with the equipment, knowledge, authority, or other tools needed for a particular task; to furnish with capability; to equip.

quote.citation: 1593, anonymous author, The Life and Death of Iacke Straw […], Act I:
quote.text: thou getteſt no more of me.For I am ſure thy Office doth not arme thee with ſuch authoritie.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 1 Peter 4:1:
quote.text: arm yourselves likewise with the same mind: for he that hath suffered in the flesh hath ceased from sin;

quote.citation: 1801(?), John Bunyan, The Pilgrim's Progress ... to which is Added, the Life and Death of the Author, page 359:
quote.text: Many following him, and, in his journeyings, he visited many at their houses, and gave them consolation, arming them with steady resolves, to be patient in suffering  and trust to God for their reward;  […]

quote.citation: 1806, William turner, An Abstract of the History of the Bible ... With questions for examination, etc, page 43:
quote.text: [God] directed them to choose out three hundred only, and, arming them with nothing but trumpets and lamps, to send them by night into the camp of the Midianites.

quote.citation: 1885, United States Congressional Serial Set, page 119:
quote.text: Q. In other words, you were commissioning men here in Cincinnati to attend the polls, arming them with authority to arrest citizens; men from outside of the city of Cincinnati to arrest citizens of the city of Cincinnati  […]

quote.citation: 2011, Meredith H. Lair, Armed with Abundance: Consumerism & Soldiering in the Vietnam War, Univ of North Carolina Press, →ISBN, page 215:
quote.text: Picture taking soothed support troops' anxieties twice over, empowering them as they navigated a strange environment, and arming them with proof that they really had served in a war.

quote.citation: 2014, Susan Fawcett, Grassroots with Readings: The Writer's Workbook, Cengage Learning, →ISBN, page 466:
quote.text: […]  and arming them with skills, work habits, and inner confidence that no one can ever take away.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To prepare (a tool, weapon, or system) for action; to activate.
(intransitive, of a tool, weapon, or system) To become prepared for action; to activate.

quote.citation: 2021 March 10, Drachinifel, 14:43 from the start, in Guadalcanal Campaign - The Big Night Battle: Night 1 (IJN 3(?) : 2 USN)‎[3], archived from the original on 17 October 2022:
quote.text: Torpedoes were loosed, but the range was too short for them to actually arm, and they bounced harmlessly off the ship as it cut loose with its secondary and antiaircraft guns, smashing anything that it could see.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cover or furnish with a plate, or with whatever will add strength, force, security, or efficiency.
(intransitive) To take up weapons; to arm oneself.

quote.citation: 1974 February 2, Igor S. V. de Goldilox-Goldilox, “Personal advertisement”, in Gay Community News, volume 1, number 32, page 14:
quote.text: Are you arming, comrade Atheists?Are you arming for the fray?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To fit (a magnet) with an armature.
